question: Is faith a feeling, a decision, or something else?
intro: Everybody says "have faith" like it's obvious what that means. Is it a feeling you either have or don't? Is it a choice? Is it believing something you can't prove? Preach My Gospel calls it the first principle of the gospel, which means if you get this one wrong, the rest wobbles. This week we figure out what it actually is.

days.q: What does the New Testament say faith is?
days.intro: Hebrews 11 is the closest thing scripture has to a definition, and it's one verse. Then read the dad in Mark 9, who says the most honest sentence in the Bible. When you read, notice that he has faith and doubt at the same time, and Jesus heals his kid anyway.
days.journal: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Which half of that sentence is louder in you right now?

days.q: What did the word mean to them?
days.intro: The Greek word is *pistis*. It means trust, or faithfulness, more than belief. When Paul says "faith in Christ" he's closer to "trusting Christ" than "believing facts about Christ." You can believe your doctor is good and still not take the medicine. Read Hebrews 11 as a list of people who *did* something, not people who felt something.
days.journal: Pick one person from Hebrews 11. What did their faith make them do?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon add?
days.intro: Alma 32 is the best explanation of faith anywhere. He doesn't define it, he tells you how to grow it. Like a seed. You plant it, you see if it grows, and the growing is the evidence. When you read, look for the experiment. He literally calls it that.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "Faith in Jesus Christ"
days.journal: Alma says try the experiment. What's one thing you've been unwilling to try because you don't have enough faith to be sure it'll work?

days.q: What do apostles say faith is?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2013. He uses the dad from Mark 9 and builds a whole talk on it. If you only read one talk this year, this might be it.
days.takeaway: His point is that you start with what faith you *have*, not what you wish you had. Hold on to what you know, and let your doubts stay doubts instead of turning them into conclusions. He says to be as candid about your questions as you need to be, but don't let the unknown crowd out what you actually do know. Faith and doubt can be in the same person at the same time, and Jesus works with that.
days.journal: Holland says hold on to what you already know. Write down three things you actually know.

days.q: If faith is a choice, why can't I just choose it?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. People say faith is a decision. Fine. But you can't just decide to believe something any more than you can decide to like a food you hate. So what part of it is a choice and what part isn't? Read a king who prays to a God he isn't sure exists, then Alma on starting with almost nothing. Don't let yourself off easy.
days.journal: Alma says you can start with just wanting to believe. Is that enough for you? What's stopping you from that much?

days.q: How do you actually build it?
days.intro: Faith grows the way a muscle grows: by using it on things you can't see the end of. Nephi built a ship without a blueprint. The brother of Jared couldn't see through the veil until he'd already made the stones. When you read, look at the order. Action, then seeing. Never the other way around.
days.journal: Pick one thing this week you'll do *before* you're sure it'll work. Write it down. That's the experiment.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the dad in Mark 9. Read the whole thing again. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Is faith a feeling, a decision, or something else? Use your own words. And say what you're going to do about it.

question: Jesus said don't worry about tomorrow. Tomorrow is a real problem. So what did He mean?
intro: "Take no thought for the morrow" is one of the most quoted lines in the Sermon on the Mount, and one of the least followed. You have bills. You have kids. You have a job that might not be there in a year. Jesus knew that too. So either He was being naive, or He meant something more specific than "don't plan." Let's find out which.

days.q: What did He actually say?
days.intro: Read the whole passage, not the one line. He's not talking about planning. He's talking about *worry*. And He gives a reason at the end that most people miss: seek the kingdom first, and the rest follows. When you read, count how many times He says "take no thought." Then find what He says to do instead.
days.journal: What's the thing you're worried about most right now? Write it down. We'll come back to it.

days.q: What did "take no thought" mean to them?
days.intro: The Greek is *merimnao*, which means to be anxious, to be pulled apart. It's not "don't think." It's "don't be torn up." And notice the audience. These were poor people. Day laborers. When Jesus said don't worry about food and clothes, He was talking to people who actually didn't know where dinner was coming from. That makes the promise heavier, not lighter. Read the widow of Zarephath, who was making her last meal when a prophet asked her to feed him first.
days.journal: Is your worry about real needs, or about wanting more than you need? Be honest.

days.q: What does the Restoration say about providing?
days.intro: Here's where it gets practical. The Lord told the early Saints the same thing, and then in the same breath told them to work. Read D&C 84, which quotes the Sermon on the Mount almost word for word and then adds instructions. Then read Nephi with a broken bow and a starving family. He trusted God *and* made a new bow. Both.
days.journal: D&C 84 is a promise to missionaries who left everything. How much of that promise applies to you? How much are you sure?

days.q: What do prophets say about worry?
days.intro: Elder Ronald A. Rasband, October 2018. He gave this talk when the world felt unstable and it's held up.

read.speaker: Ronald A. Rasband
read.section: Read the whole thing. It's short.

days.takeaway: His point is that "be not troubled" is a commandment, not a suggestion, and Jesus gave it right before describing wars, earthquakes, and everything else that's coming. The peace isn't because things will be fine. It's because He's in charge of the things that won't be. Rasband lists the things that anchor you: covenants, the Spirit, the prophet, and doing what you already know to do.
days.journal: Rasband says peace comes from what you're anchored to, not what's happening around you. What are you actually anchored to right now?

days.q: But Paul said provide for your family or you're worse than an unbeliever. So which is it?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Jesus says don't worry about food. Paul says if you don't provide for your family you've denied the faith. The Lord told Joseph Smith that the idler shall not eat the bread of the laborer. So is it "trust God" or "work hard"? Read these and figure out where the line is between worry and responsibility.
days.journal: Where's the line for you between responsibly planning and being torn apart by worry? Where are you crossing it?

days.q: How do you actually stop worrying?
days.intro: Jesus gives the how in the same passage, but it's easy to miss. Seek the kingdom *first*. Not instead. First. And Paul gives the mechanics: pray about it, be thankful, and let the peace come. Then read Nephi, who had every reason to worry and describes what he does instead. When you read, look for what replaces the worry.
days.journal: Go back to what you wrote on Day 1. Pray about it tonight, specifically. Then write one sentence about what you'll do tomorrow that's seeking the kingdom first.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the lilies. Read it once more with the week behind you.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What did Jesus mean by "take no thought for the morrow"? And what's your worry from Day 1 look like now?

question: Why does Jesus heal some people and not others?
intro: Jesus healed a lot of people. He also walked past a lot of people. At the pool of Bethesda there were crowds of sick people and He healed one guy. Alma watched women and children burn and didn't stop it. If God can heal, and doesn't, that's a real question, and "His ways are higher" is not a full answer. Don't expect one this week. Expect to think harder.

days.q: Who did He heal, and how?
days.intro: Read a run of healings from Matthew 8. Notice the variety. Some people ask. Some are brought. One guy's servant isn't even in the room. Then read Bethesda. There's a crowd, and Jesus heals one man, and He doesn't explain why him.
days.journal: At Bethesda there were many sick and one got healed. If you'd been one of the others, what would you have thought?

days.q: What did healing mean in their world?
days.intro: Sickness in first-century Judea wasn't just physical. Lepers were unclean and cut off from the temple and their families. Being healed meant getting your life back. And people assumed sickness meant sin. Jesus's disciples asked Him about that directly, and His answer is one of the most important things He ever said about suffering.
days.journal: The disciples assumed the blind man or his parents sinned. Whose suffering have you quietly assumed they earned?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon add?
days.intro: Two stories. Alma and Amulek watch believers burn and Alma says the Spirit told him not to stop it. Then Alma's people in bondage, who aren't freed but are strengthened. When you read, look for what the Lord does *instead* of fixing it.
days.journal: Alma 7:12 says Christ took on our infirmities so He'd know how to help. Does that change anything about the times He doesn't heal? Why or why not?

days.q: What do apostles say about the unfairness of it?
days.intro: Elder Dale G. Renlund, April 2021. He's a heart doctor. He's watched people die who shouldn't have. He didn't dodge this one.
days.takeaway: His point is that unfairness is real, it's not your imagination, and God doesn't ask you to pretend it isn't. What He promises is that Jesus Christ will make everything right eventually, and that in the meantime He'll be with you in it. Renlund says the Savior's suffering wasn't fair either, and that's exactly why He understands yours.
days.journal: Renlund says it's okay to call unfairness what it is. What's the unfair thing you've been trying not to be angry about?

days.q: If He can heal and doesn't, is He choosing not to?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, and I'm not going to soften it. God has the power. Someone you love needed healing and didn't get it. So either He couldn't or He wouldn't. Read these. D&C 42 says some people are "appointed unto death," which means there's a plan you can't see. That's either comforting or infuriating depending on the day. Let it be both. Then read Martha and Mary, who both said it to His face.
days.journal: Write the name of someone you prayed for who wasn't healed. What do you actually believe about why?

days.q: What do you do while you wait to be healed?
days.intro: Sometimes the healing is the thing. Sometimes the healing is what you become while you're not healed. Nephi says his heart groans because of his flesh and then decides to trust anyway. Paul got told no three times and calls it grace. When you read, look for what they do with the no.
days.journal: Who around you is waiting to be healed, physically or otherwise? What can you do this week that's the "strengthened in bondage" kind of help?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Bethesda. Read it once more, and then read the name you wrote on Day 5.
days.journal: Answer the week's question as honestly as you can: Why does Jesus heal some and not others? It's fine if the answer is "I don't know, but here's what I trust."

question: Repentance. Why does it feel like punishment when God calls it a gift?
intro: Say the word "repent" and most people flinch. It sounds like a scolding. But the scriptures call it a gift, prophets call it joyful, and the word itself doesn't mean "feel terrible." It means turn around. Change your mind. Get better. This week connects back to Week 4: if perfect means complete, repentance is how you get more complete. It's self-discovery followed by a commitment, not a penalty box.

days.q: What did Jesus say about rest?
days.intro: Read what you wrote on Day 7 of Week 4 first. You rewrote "be ye therefore perfect" in your own words. Now read Jesus's invitation in Matthew 11. He's talking to people worn out by religion. His answer isn't "try harder." It's "come to me." That's the door repentance walks through.
days.journal: When you hear the word "repent," what's the first feeling? Write it down. We'll see if it changes.

days.q: What does the word actually mean?
days.intro: Greek: *metanoia*. A change of mind, a new way of seeing. Hebrew: *shuv*. To turn, to return, to come home. Neither one means "feel bad." Feeling bad is sometimes part of it, but it's not the thing. The thing is the turn. Read Alma asking what turning looks like, then read what Peter said to a crowd that had just realized they'd killed the Messiah.
days.journal: If repentance is a change of mind, what's one thing you think about wrong that needs changing? Not a sin. A way of seeing.

days.q: What did Alma do with his repentance?
days.intro: Alma the Younger is the case study. He was in real pain for three days. But read what he does afterward. He doesn't sit around feeling sorry. He spends the rest of his life building something. When you read, look at the ratio: how many verses on the pain, how many on what came next.
days.journal: Alma's pain was three days. His work was thirty years. What's something you've been stuck feeling bad about that you should have turned into work by now?

days.q: What do prophets say repentance is?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, April 2019. He gave this to the priesthood session and told them straight that repentance is not a punishment.

read.talk: We Can Do Better and Be Better
read.speaker: Russell M. Nelson

days.takeaway: His point is that repentance is one of the most hopeful words in scripture, and the Greek means changing your mind, your knowledge, your spirit, even your breathing. He says nothing is more liberating or more ennobling. And he's clear that it's daily, not just for big sins: "do better and be better" is the whole assignment.
days.journal: Nelson says repentance is daily. What's one thing you could do better tomorrow that has nothing to do with a "sin"?

days.q: Then where does sorrow fit?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If repentance is about becoming, why does the Church talk about confession, restitution, forsaking? Why does Paul talk about godly sorrow? Because there *is* a kind of sorrow that's part of it. But there's also a kind that isn't. Paul separates them. King Benjamin's people felt the first kind and it led somewhere. Read these and figure out the difference.
days.journal: Paul says one kind of sorrow leads to repentance and the other leads to death. Which kind have you been carrying?

days.q: What's the next thing to get better at?
days.intro: This is the self-discovery part. Not a sin inventory. Zacchaeus climbs a tree just to see Jesus, gets called by name, and on the spot decides who he's going to be from now on. When you read, look at how specific his commitment is. Then pick one.
days.journal: Pick one thing to get better at. Not a habit to quit. Something to become. Write it down and write what you'll do about it this week. That's repentance.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Read your Day 1 answer. Then read the invitation in Matthew 11 one more time.
days.journal: Rewrite the word "repent" in your own words, the way you rewrote "perfect" in Week 4. Then answer: why did it ever feel like punishment?

question: Why did Jesus teach in parables instead of just explaining?
intro: Jesus was the best teacher who ever lived and He mostly told stories. Farmers, sheep, coins, seeds. The disciples asked Him why, and His answer is strange: so that some people *wouldn't* understand. That doesn't sound like the Jesus we sing about. This week is about why He taught the way He did, and what that means for how you're supposed to learn.

days.q: What's the first parable, and what did He say about it?
days.intro: The sower is the parable about parables. Jesus tells it, then explains why He uses them, then explains the story itself. Read all three parts. When you read, notice that the story is about *how people listen*. That's not an accident.
days.journal: Four kinds of soil. Which one are you most of the time? Not which one do you want to be.

days.q: How did stories work in His world?
days.intro: Rabbis in Jesus's day taught with *mashal*, which means comparison or riddle. A parable wasn't a fable with a moral at the end. It was a puzzle. You had to work it out, and the working was the lesson. Nathan used one on David and David convicted himself before he realized who the story was about. Read that.
days.journal: Nathan's story worked because David didn't know it was about him. Which of Jesus's parables have you been assuming is about someone else?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say about how God teaches?
days.intro: Alma 32 is a parable too, about a seed. But the key verse for this week is about *why* God gives some people more than others. Alma 12 says it's about what you do with what you've got. And in 3 Nephi 17 Jesus sees the people can't take it all in and sends them home to ponder. When you read, look for the rule: what earns you more understanding?
days.journal: Jesus told them to go home and ponder before He said more. What has He already told you that you never went home and pondered?

days.q: How does a modern apostle teach with a parable?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2012. He takes one parable, the laborers in the vineyard, and turns it inside out. Read it and watch how he does it. That's how a parable is supposed to work on you.

read.speaker: Jeffrey R. Holland
read.note: Read Matthew 20:1-16 first if you don't know the story.

days.takeaway: His point is that the parable isn't about wages. It's about the people who worked all day and got angry that the latecomers got the same. Holland says that's most of us. We keep score. And God doesn't. He pays everyone in full because He's generous, not because He's fair by our math.
days.journal: Holland says we keep score on people who came late. Who are you keeping score on?

days.q: Was Jesus actually hiding truth from people?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Matthew 13:11 says it's given to some to know the mysteries and not to others. That sounds like God picking favorites. Read it again with Isaiah behind it. Then read Jesus's own explanation for why the same story lands differently on different people. Is He hiding truth, or protecting people from truth they'd be accountable for and reject?
days.journal: D&C 50:24 says light grows brighter if you receive it. Is there truth you've been given that you've been sitting on? What would receiving it look like?

days.q: How do you get more out of a parable?
days.intro: Simple test. Read one and ask: who am I in this story? Not who should I be. Who am I. Jesus's parables always have a character you'd rather not be. Read three short ones today and find yourself in each one.
days.journal: For each of the three, one line: who were you in it?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the sower. Read it once more, and then your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did Jesus teach in parables? And what kind of listener does that require you to be?

question: Easter. Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn't God just forgive?
intro: It's Easter week. Everybody knows Jesus died for our sins. Fewer people can say why He *had* to. If God is all-powerful and loves us, why not just forgive? Why does someone have to bleed for it? The Book of Mormon takes this question head on, and the answer isn't what most people assume. This is the center of everything, so slow down.

days.q: What actually happened that week?
days.intro: Start with the story. Read the triumphal entry and then jump to the arrest. Notice how fast the crowd turns. Notice that Jesus knew all of it and walked into it anyway.
days.journal: Before this week, what would you say if a kid asked you why Jesus had to die? Write it down.

days.q: What did "atonement" mean to them?
days.intro: Hebrew: *kaphar*, to cover. On the Day of Atonement the high priest covered the sins of Israel with the blood of an animal. Every Jew understood that sin cost something and something died for it. Jesus died during Passover, when lambs were being killed all over Jerusalem. Nobody in that city would have missed the point. Read Leviticus, then Isaiah, then John the Baptist.
days.journal: Think of a time someone else paid for something you did. How did it feel to watch them pay it?

days.q: Why couldn't God just forgive?
days.intro: Here's the answer nobody gives at church because it takes too long. Alma explains it to his son. Justice is real. It's not a rule God made up; it's part of how things are. If God ignored it, He'd stop being God. So mercy can't just cancel justice. Something has to satisfy it. Read Alma 42 slowly. It's the most important chapter this week.
days.journal: Alma says if mercy robbed justice, God would cease to be God. Does that make sense to you, or does it still feel like He could have found another way?

days.q: What do apostles say about justice and mercy?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2015. He tells a story about two brothers on a cliff and then explains the Atonement through it. Read it.

read.talk: Where Justice, Love, and Mercy Meet
read.speaker: Jeffrey R. Holland

days.takeaway: His point is that the Atonement isn't a transaction where God was paid off. It's an act of love that reaches down to where you actually are. He says the Savior's suffering was voluntary and it was for *you*, personally, not humanity in general. And he doesn't clean up the cross. He says the pain was real and the price was paid in full.
days.journal: Holland says the cross reaches to where you are. Where are you right now that feels too far down for that?

days.q: Was the Father cruel to require it?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, and people avoid it. If the Father required His Son to suffer like that, what does that say about the Father? Read the plan from the Son's own mouth: He volunteered. Read what Jesus said in Gethsemane. Then read what He said about it afterward, in D&C 19, which is the only place in scripture where the Savior describes His own suffering in the first person.
days.journal: D&C 19 is Jesus telling you what it cost Him and why. Read verse 16 again. Now write what you'd say to Him about it.

days.q: What are you supposed to do with a gift that big?
days.intro: The Atonement is free and it also asks something. Both. The Nephites who survived the destruction heard the Savior's own voice tell them what He wanted. Moroni ends the whole Book of Mormon with the how. When you read, look for the verbs. What does He actually ask you to do?
days.journal: 3 Nephi 9:20 asks for a broken heart. What's the thing you're holding onto that would have to break?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Easter Sunday. Read the resurrection first thing. Then read what you wrote on Day 1.
days.journal: Answer the week's question the way you'd say it to a kid now: Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn't God just forgive?

question: Why did Peter sink?
intro: Peter walked on water. Actually walked on it. Then he sank. We usually treat that as a failure story, but he's the only one who got out of the boat. Eleven guys stayed put. So what happened between the first step and the sinking? And what did Jesus mean when He asked "wherefore didst thou doubt?" This is faith in motion, which is the only kind that counts.

days.q: What happened on the water?
days.intro: Read Matthew's version, which has Peter in it. Then Mark's, which doesn't mention Peter at all but has a detail Matthew leaves out about *why* they were afraid. When you read Matthew, find the exact moment Peter starts sinking. What changed?
days.journal: Peter was fine until he looked at the wind. What's the "wind" you look at that makes you sink?

days.q: What was that night actually like?
days.intro: The Sea of Galilee sits in a bowl and storms come off the hills fast. The disciples had been rowing against the wind since evening. It was the fourth watch, between three and six in the morning. They'd been at it for nine hours. They were fishermen. They knew exactly how much trouble they were in. Then a figure walks toward them on the water, and they think it's a ghost. Read Mark again for the loaves detail, and then read Job, because God has a history with the sea.
days.journal: Mark says they were afraid because they didn't understand the loaves. What miracle have you already seen that you've forgotten when the next storm hits?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say about the trial of faith?
days.intro: Moroni says you don't get the witness until *after* the trial of your faith. Peter got the witness after he sank, not before he stepped. That's the order. Read these and look for what comes first and what comes second.
days.journal: Nephi went into Jerusalem "not knowing beforehand." When have you stepped out not knowing? What happened?

days.q: What do apostles say about faith and choosing?
days.intro: Elder Neil L. Andersen, October 2015. He takes on the idea that faith just happens to you.

read.talk: Faith Is Not by Chance, but by Choice
read.speaker: Neil L. Andersen

days.takeaway: His point is that faith doesn't fall on you by accident and it doesn't leave you by accident either. It grows or shrinks based on what you choose to do with your questions, your attention, and your feet. He says when doubts come you have a choice about where to look, and where you look is where you go. Peter looked at the wind. That was a choice too.
days.journal: Andersen says you choose where you look. Where have you been looking lately, and what's that doing to your faith?

days.q: Was Jesus criticizing Peter?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. "Wherefore didst thou doubt?" sounds like a rebuke. Peter did more than anyone else in that boat and got called out for it. Is doubt a sin? Or was Jesus asking a real question? Read how Jesus treats other doubters. The dad in Mark 9 doubts out loud and gets his kid back. Thomas doubts and gets a private invitation. Oliver Cowdery doubts and gets told to remember.
days.journal: Do you think Jesus was disappointed in Peter, or asking him a question he needed to answer? What's the difference, and which would you rather hear?

days.q: How do you get out of the boat?
days.intro: Peter asked first. "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come." He didn't just jump. He asked, got told yes, then went. That's the pattern. Then when he sank he did the one thing that saved him: he yelled for help immediately. When you read, look for what the Lord tells people to do when they're afraid.
days.journal: What's the thing you'd do if the Lord told you "come"? Ask Him this week. Then write down what you'll do if the answer is yes.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the water. Read it one more time, all the way to the end where they worship Him. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did Peter sink? And what's the real lesson, the sinking or the stepping?
